extracted.intended_audience: naturalists/anatomists/physicians (Fellows of the Royal Society and 17th-century comparative anatomists)
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed anatomical and comparative description intended to discriminate the lumbricus latus (tapeworm) from other worms by morphological, behavioural, and functional features based on dissection and microscope observation. Includes measurements, variation among specimens, and functional hypotheses (feeding, attachment, motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Being flat (body dorsoventrally flattened)
rubrics_metrics.description: The body is flat (hence called lumbricus latus or tape-worm), which sufficiently distinguishes it from other worms that are round (teretes/ascarides) or have other shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flatness distinguishes it from common intestinal worms; no known worms outside the body are thus flat. Use gross inspection of cross-section/shape to separate lumbricus latus from round worms and earth-worms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joints: distinctive annulation and overlapping edges
rubrics_metrics.description: Joints/annuli are arranged so the extreme edges of one joint come over the next, with edges sometimes plain, sometimes crenated/indented; direction of roughness (tail-to-head rough, head-to-tail smooth) is diagnostic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe how joints interlock and whether edges project over the following joint — this helps locate the head and distinguish species. Note variation: some joints plain, others serrated; contraction/extension alters apparent dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproportion of extremes (head vs tail)
rubrics_metrics.description: One extreme (the head end) is much smaller than the other (tail end); joints toward the head are vastly shorter than those toward the tail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure relative widths and joint lengths along the body: in long specimens the head-end joints may be many more per inch than tail-end. Be cautious: observers sometimes mistake tail for head if not accounting for joint-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vast length (often convoluted in gut)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specimens can be extremely long (many yards to reported hundreds of feet) and lie convoluted in the intestines rather than extended straight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume short voided pieces are separate individuals; total length may be much greater when convoluted. Record measured lengths and joint counts (example: specimen 24 feet with 507 joints) to characterize specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head beset with hooked spikes/claspers
rubrics_metrics.description: The head (as observed with good microscopes) is thickly beset with two orders of spikes or hooks: larger hooks arising from the middle and smaller shorter spikes issuing midway; head can evert/retract by contracting/expanding the neck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use magnification to examine head morphology; the hooks appear to fasten into the intestinal coat and are implicated in attachment and pain. Presence/arrangement of hooks is a key species-character and explains difficulty of expulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of many lateral protuberant orifices (interpreted as mouths) in each joint
rubrics_metrics.description: Each joint bears protuberant orifices (papilla-like with a central foramen) usually placed alternately on right and left edges, sometimes two or three successive on same side; these are argued to function as mouths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence for oral function: joints often turgid with chylous juice; afflicted hosts show appetite/thirst and emaciation; no other suitable mouth is observed; orifices readily admit a hog's bristle and may exude chylous fluid in spirits. Record position (edge vs flat), alternation pattern, and size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two distinct kinds/placements of orifices
rubrics_metrics.description: Orifices occur in two sorts: (a) protuberant papillae placed about the middle of the joint edges (most common), and (b) protuberances placed about the middle of the flat of the joint toward the upper part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish which type is present when describing a specimen; the transverse black line sometimes notes the edge-type. Variation in orifice placement is taxonomically informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument-from-function for orifices being mouths
rubrics_metrics.description: Four lines of argument are given that these side-orifices are mouths: (1) worms are often turgid with chyle; (2) hosts exhibit great appetite/thirst and emaciation; (3) no other mouth capable of ingesting sufficient chyle is observed; (4) no other function (vents, lungs) fits the size/arrangement of these openings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use functional evidence (turgidity, host symptoms, absence of alternative feeding organ) to interpret morphological structures; consider and rebut alternative interpretations (excrement vents, bronchial-like structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pieces of worm remain alive when broken off
rubrics_metrics.description: When parts of the body are broken off they may remain alive and thrive for some time, implying each broken unit has capacity for sustaining itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe vitality of voided pieces (e.g., survival in water or spirit briefly); this supports hypothesis of multiple mouths and autonomous feeding in segments. Note as diagnostic behaviour distinguishing true animals from mere intestinal membrane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal generation and distinct sexes (sexual differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lumbricus latus exhibits univocal generation with distinct male and female sexes; organs of each are conspicuous and plainly contrived, unlike hermaphroditic earth-worms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissect to examine reproductive organs and sexual differentiation; use this reproductive anatomy to distinguish lumbricus latus from hermaphroditic annelids like earth-worms and leeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion by concerted contraction of joints and scale-like prominences aiding progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressive motion arises from contracting/shortening joints in several places simultaneously; the prominence of the former joint over the latter functions like scales/feet and promotes forward movement; body can change form (flat to round, concave/convex) during motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe live specimens (or freshly voided) for patterns of contraction and surface prominences; note that simultaneous contractions at spaced intervals help locomotion in very long animals and that shape changes are frequent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head placement and adhesion to intestinal coat (practical identification of anterior end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissections show the smaller extreme, which adheres firmly to the inward coat of the intestine (often toward the duodenum), is the head; broader end is free toward the rectum — contradicting some earlier figures which misidentified ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track the worm through the gut to the smallest extreme and test for firm adhesion to identify the anterior/head end. Be wary of earlier illustrations that may have reversed head/tail based on external appearance alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intraspecific and interspecific variation (multiple sorts/species)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is substantial variation among specimens: joint size and proportions, placement of orifices, serration vs plain edges, overall length, and head form — implying more than one sort/species of taenia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record a suite of characters (joint counts per inch, orifice placement, head morphology, color, turgidity, measurements) rather than single traits. Note that contraction state affects apparent dimensions; compare multiple specimens from different hosts to assess variation.
